theory.heading: Recognise line conventions
theory.body: Technical drawings use different line types to communicate different kinds of information. Visible outlines show edges that can be seen from the viewing direction and are usually drawn clearly. Hidden detail lines show edges or features that are behind a visible surface and are commonly represented by short, even dashes. Centre lines identify the centre or axis of a circular or symmetrical feature. Reading each line by its convention helps prevent one type of information from being mistaken for another.

theory.heading: Separate dimensions and construction lines
theory.body: Dimension lines communicate the extent of a written measurement and connect it to the relevant feature. The written dimension controls intended size, not the apparent length of the drawn line. Light projection or construction lines are temporary drawing guides used to transfer positions and maintain relationships between views. They should remain lighter than visible outlines so they do not appear to be part of the object. Each line type has a distinct purpose, so its meaning must be read in context.

theory.heading: Align features across views
theory.body: Related views represent the same object from different directions, so shared features should align. A feature shown in the front view should connect logically with its position in the plan and side views. Light projection lines can help compare these positions. Alignment does not mean that a feature looks identical in every view. It may appear as an outline, hidden detail or centre position depending on the viewing direction. When a line or alignment is unclear, compare the related views and written information, then ask rather than guessing. Current school SOPs and teacher directions control all actual workshop activity.

questions.question: Which line type shows an edge that can be seen from the viewing direction?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A visible outline represents an edge that can be seen in that view.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Recognise line conventions and focus on the line used for seen edges.

questions.question: Which convention commonly represents a feature behind a visible surface?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Hidden detail lines commonly use short, even dashes to represent unseen features.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Recognise line conventions and identify how hidden detail is represented.

questions.question: What does a centre line identify?
choices: The outside edge of every object
The centre or axis of a circular or symmetrical feature
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Centre lines identify centres or axes in circular and symmetrical features.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Recognise line conventions and focus on the purpose of a centre line.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a dimension line?
choices: To mark the centre of a feature
To connect a written measurement to a feature
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Dimension lines show the extent and location of written measurement information.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Separate dimensions and construction lines and identify how written measurements are linked to features.

questions.question: What controls the intended size shown on a technical drawing?
choices: The apparent length of the dimension line
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The written dimension controls intended size rather than the line appearance.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Separate dimensions and construction lines and focus on what controls size.

questions.question: Why are projection or construction lines drawn lightly?
choices: They are guides and should not look like object outlines
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Light lines guide drawing and alignment without being confused with visible object edges.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Separate dimensions and construction lines and compare guide lines with visible outlines.

questions.question: What do light projection lines help transfer between related views?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Projection lines help maintain matching feature positions across views.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Separate dimensions and construction lines and identify what the guide lines transfer.

questions.question: Why should shared features align across related views?
choices: The views represent the same object from different directions
Each view shows a different product
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Alignment connects the same feature across different viewing directions.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Align features across views and focus on why views are related.

questions.question: Why might one feature use different line conventions across views?
choices: Its actual form changes between views
Its visibility changes with the viewing direction
The feature moves on the drawing
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A feature may be visible, hidden or centred depending on the direction of view.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Align features across views and identify why the same feature can appear differently.

questions.question: What should a student do when a line or alignment remains unclear?
choices: Compare related views and written information, then ask
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Cross-checking and asking prevents unsupported drawing interpretations.
questions.retryFeedback: Review the final sentences of Align features across views and identify the response to uncertainty.

written.prompt: Explain how three different line conventions and alignment across related views help communicate an object clearly.
written.sentenceStarter: A visible outline shows ___, a hidden detail line shows ___, and a centre or projection line helps ___. Related views align because ___.
written.example: A visible outline shows an edge that can be seen, a hidden detail line shows a feature behind a surface, and a projection line helps transfer positions. Related views align because they represent the same object from different directions.
